description: Read-only fallback snapshot of 34 reviewed verse-specific historical textual source associations covering 23 unique verses, refreshed from the live database on 2026-11-08. Database is authoritative; 4Q225 includes restored fragmentary readings and textual similarity is not proof of dependence.

records.approx_date: 2nd century CE
records.source_locator: Protoevangelium of James §4 (Anna's vow)
records.parallel_summary: Anna promises to dedicate her future child to the Lord, whether male or female; Qur'an 3:35 presents Mary's mother dedicating her unborn child.
records.similarity_note: Both narrate a maternal vow to dedicate a child to divine service.
records.difference_note: The apocryphal account names Anna and Joachim; Qur'an 3:35 does not name the parents.
records.source_edition: New Advent English translation, Protoevangelium of James, §4
records.verification_note: Compared the maternal vow in §4 with Qur'an 3:35. This is a narrative parallel, not evidence of direct literary borrowing.

records.approx_date: 2nd century CE
records.source_locator: Protoevangelium of James §8 (Mary fed by an angel; Zacharias)
records.parallel_summary: Mary resides in the temple, receives food from an angel, and Zacharias appears as a priest; Qur'an 3:37 describes Zakariya's care of Mary and unexpected provision.
records.similarity_note: Both associate Mary with sacred precincts, Zacharias/Zakariya, and extraordinary provision.
records.difference_note: The apocryphal text explicitly attributes food to an angel; the Qur'an records Mary's reply that provision is from Allah without naming an angel as its carrier.
records.source_edition: New Advent English translation, Protoevangelium of James, §8
records.verification_note: Read §8 and compared its specific food and Zacharias details with Qur'an 3:37; the accounts are related but not identical.

records.approx_date: 2nd century CE
records.source_locator: Infancy Gospel of Thomas, First Greek Form §2 (clay sparrows)
records.parallel_summary: The young Jesus shapes twelve sparrows from clay and makes them fly; Qur'an 3:49 recounts Jesus forming a bird from clay and breathing into it by God's permission.
records.similarity_note: Both texts feature Jesus making living birds from clay.
records.difference_note: The Infancy Gospel describes twelve sparrows, a Sabbath dispute and clapping; the Qur'an emphasizes breathing and God's permission, without those details.
records.source_edition: New Advent English translation, First Greek Form, §2
records.verification_note: Verified the clay-sparrow episode in the First Greek Form §2 and compared it to Qur'an 3:49. Similarity alone does not prove borrowing.

records.approx_date: The work commonly called the Gospel of Peter is often assigned to the second century CE, but the identification of the extant Akhmim text with the gospel known to Serapion c. 200 CE is debated. The Akhmim codex witness is palaeographically dated approximately seventh–ninth century CE, not the date of original composition (Paul Foster, New Testament Studies 52.1 [2006], 1–28).
records.source_locator: Gospel of Peter (Akhmim fragment), §§4–6 in the conventional chapter divisions, especially §4 (crucifixion) and §6 (body removed and buried)
records.parallel_summary: Qur’an 4:157 denies that Jesus was killed or crucified by those making the claim. The surviving Gospel of Peter passion narrative explicitly says in §4 that the Lord was crucified between two criminals and describes his removal from the cross and burial in §6. This is a documented textual CONTRAST about crucifixion, not an account that independently denies it.
records.similarity_note: Both texts address the claimed crucifixion of Jesus, but their explicit claims differ. Gospel of Peter §4 says he was crucified; Qur’an 4:157 denies it.
records.difference_note: The Gospel of Peter §4 says Jesus was silent as though feeling no pain, and §5 says he was taken up; these debated docetic-sounding expressions do not erase its explicit statement of crucifixion in §4 or the burial in §6. No claim of direct borrowing or shared denial of crucifixion is justified.
records.source_edition: J. Armitage Robinson, English translation of the Akhmim fragment, reproduced in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 9, The Gospel According to Peter, §§4–6; https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1001.htm . Manuscript and dating caution: Paul Foster, “Are There Any Early Fragments of the So-Called Gospel of Peter?” New Testament Studies 52.1 (2006), pp. 1–28, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0028688506000014 .
records.verification_note: 2026-11-02 batch 7: checked actual Gospel of Peter §§4–6 at https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1001.htm : §4 explicitly narrates crucifixion, §5 includes “taken up,” §6 removal of nails and burial. Checked Paul Foster (2006) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0028688506000014 for disputed identification and seventh–ninth century Akhmim manuscript dating. Classified strictly as a CONTRAST to Qur’an 4:157, not a docetic denial of crucifixion or evidence of dependence. Distinguish proposed composition date from extant witness.

records.approx_date: Commonly dated to the second century CE; extant Greek witnesses and recensions are later.
records.source_locator: Infancy Gospel of Thomas, First Greek Form §2 (clay sparrows)
records.parallel_summary: The First Greek Form §2 describes the young Jesus forming twelve sparrows from clay and making them fly; Qur’an 5:110 recalls Jesus shaping a bird from clay and breathing into it by God’s permission.
records.similarity_note: Both passages describe Jesus giving life to a clay bird.
records.difference_note: The apocryphal narrative mentions twelve sparrows, a Sabbath dispute, and clapping; Qur’an 5:110 emphasizes breathing and repeated divine permission, without those details.
records.source_edition: New Advent English translation, First Greek Form, §2
records.verification_note: Compared the First Greek Form §2 (clay birds and clapping) with Qur’an 5:110 (clay bird and breathing by divine permission). Shared motif does not establish direct dependence; composition and surviving manuscript dates differ.

records.source_title: Life of Adam and Eve Vita Adae et Evae
records.approx_date: Tradition often dated 1st–2nd century CE; surviving recensions and manuscripts later
records.source_locator: Latin Life of Adam and Eve (Vita Adae et Evae) §§12–16, especially §§13–15
records.parallel_summary: The angels are told to worship Adam; Satan refuses and is expelled. Qur'an 7:11 commands prostration before Adam, while 7:12 explains Iblis's refusal.
records.similarity_note: Both narratives contain an instruction to honor Adam and Satan's refusal.
records.difference_note: The Latin Vita cites Satan's priority of creation; Qur'an 7:12 specifically contrasts fire and clay. Manuscript and redaction histories are complex.
records.source_edition: R. H. Charles, The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament (1913), Latin Vita §§12–16
records.verification_note: Checked Latin Vita §§12–16 (especially §§13–15); linked to Qur'an 7:11 with the refusal explained in the following Qur'anic verse 7:12. Composition date and extant versions must not be conflated.

records.approx_date: The Syriac Cave of Treasures is commonly treated as a late antique composition; Sergey Minov (2017) argues for a date between the middle of the sixth century and the first decades of the seventh century, a range that can overlap the Qur’anic period. This is a proposed composition date, not the date of the surviving Syriac manuscript witness or E. A. Wallis Budge’s 1927 English translation. No demonstrated direct dependence.
records.source_locator: Cave of Treasures, First Thousand Years (Adam to Yared), part 7, “The Revolt of Satan, and the Battle in Heaven,” opening paragraph; Budge 1927 translation, Syriac manuscript fol. 5b col. 2 (continuing toward fol. 6a col. 1)
records.parallel_summary: Qur’an 7:11 depicts the angels commanded to prostrate before Adam and Iblis refusing. In the Syriac Cave of Treasures, First Thousand Years part 7, Satan refuses to honor Adam, claiming that he is fire and spirit while Adam is dust, and he falls from heaven. This is a specific narrative-motif parallel; it does not establish a demonstrably earlier textual source or direct borrowing.
records.similarity_note: Both narratives explicitly connect Satan’s refusal to honor Adam with his claimed superiority over the earth-formed human; the Syriac text says Satan is fire and spirit and Adam is dust. The Qur’an gives the fire-versus-clay rationale explicitly in 7:12, immediately after 7:11.
records.difference_note: Cave of Treasures frames Satan as prince of a lower angelic order who demands worship for himself, and places the event in a Christian sacred-history account. Qur’an 7:11–12 frames a command to angels, Iblis’s refusal, and God’s interrogation. Dates and transmission histories differ; similarity is not proof of direct literary dependence.
records.source_edition: E. A. Wallis Budge, trans., The Book of the Cave of Treasures (London: Religious Tract Society, 1927), “The First Thousand Years,” part 7 (“The Revolt of Satan, and the Battle in Heaven”), opening paragraph, fol. 5b col. 2; https://www.wisdomlib.org/christianity/book/the-book-of-the-cave-of-treasures/d/doc1561883.html . Composition analysis: Sergey Minov, “Date and Provenance of the Syriac Cave of Treasures: A Reappraisal,” Hugoye 20.1 (2017), 129–229, https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:4d0383ed-4d93-467d-a6f2-7d97988aeb94 .
records.verification_note: 2026-11-02 batch 7 continuation: checked the main translated Syriac narrative (not Budge’s later comparative editorial notes) in Cave of Treasures, First Thousand Years part 7, opening paragraph at https://www.wisdomlib.org/christianity/book/the-book-of-the-cave-of-treasures/d/doc1561883.html . It explicitly says Satan would not worship Adam because Satan was fire and spirit and Adam was dust; compares with Qur’an 7:11–12. Reviewed scholarly dating by Sergey Minov (2017), https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:4d0383ed-4d93-467d-a6f2-7d97988aeb94 . Verified as a specific narrative parallel, not evidence of pre-Qur’anic availability or direct borrowing; composition date distinct from surviving witnesses and Budge 1927 edition.

records.approx_date: Likely composed in the second century BCE; surviving textual witnesses and modern translations are later.
records.source_locator: Book of Jubilees 5:19, 5:23 (R. H. Charles translation, 1917)
records.parallel_summary: Jubilees 5:19 says Noah’s sons were saved on his account; 5:23 describes the ark entry. Qur’an 11:42–43 instead recounts Noah calling to a son who refuses to board and is drowned.
records.similarity_note: Both narrate Noah’s family during the Flood and the ark.
records.difference_note: Jubilees says Noah’s sons were saved and does not narrate the refusal-and-drowning scene of Qur’an 11:42–43. The passages do not identify the same named son.
records.source_edition: R. H. Charles (trans.), The Book of Jubilees (SPCK, London, 1917), chapter 5
records.verification_note: Checked Jubilees 5:19 and 5:23 in the R. H. Charles 1917 translation (Sefaria and the Charles text) against Qur’an 11:42–43. Classified as a textual contrast, not borrowing. The composition date is distinct from extant manuscripts and the English translation.

records.source_title: Gregory of Tours, Glory of the Martyrs (Seven Sleepers of Ephesus)
records.approx_date: Composed in the late sixth century CE, before the Qur’an; the linked Acta Sanctorum edition and English rendering are much later. Surviving manuscripts and editions must not be confused with the original composition.
records.source_locator: Gregory of Tours, Liber in gloria martyrum (Glory of the Martyrs), ch. 94 in modern editions (ch. 95 in the Acta Sanctorum numbering), Seven Sleepers of Ephesus
records.parallel_summary: Gregory describes faithful young men of Ephesus who withdrew to a cave, slept for many years, and later awoke; Qur’an 18:9 introduces the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription, whose narrative continues in 18:10–26.
records.similarity_note: Both traditions concern religiously faithful youths sheltered in a cave, an extraordinary long sleep, and a written inscription or record associated with the cave.
records.difference_note: Gregory identifies seven youths, Ephesus, Decius, Theodosius, and a lead tablet; Qur’an 18:9–26 does not name the emperors or city, reports disagreement over the number, and mentions a dog. These differences do not demonstrate direct dependence.
records.source_edition: Gregory of Tours, De gloria martyrum, ch. 94 (modern numbering); quoted as ch. 95 in Acta Sanctorum, 27 July, preliminary commentary § IV, nos. 23–25; cf. B. Krusch, MGH Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum 1.2, pp. 100–101.
records.verification_note: Reviewed Gregory’s quoted passage in Acta Sanctorum (27 July, preliminary commentary § IV, nos. 23–25), including the cave, long sleep, lead tablet and waking, against Qur’an 18:9–26. Chapter numbering differs across editions (94 modern; 95 in this older compilation). The online page is a later editorial reproduction, not a sixth-century manuscript; the Acta Sanctorum editor’s anti-Islamic polemic is not evidence for literary dependence. Classified only as a documented narrative parallel.

records.approx_date: Often dated c. 629–630 CE (early 7th century); precise composition and redaction debated. Surviving manuscripts and Budge's 1889 edition are later; not demonstrably prior to every Qur'anic passage.
records.source_type: Syriac Christian Alexander legend / apocalyptic narrative
records.source_locator: A Christian Legend concerning Alexander, E. A. Wallis Budge (1889), English translation pp. 151–154, especially pp. 152–153 (Gog/Magog named; request and iron/brass gate); Syriac edition pp. 265–268.
records.parallel_summary: In Qur'an 18:94, people report the destructive activity of Gog and Magog and ask Dhū al-Qarnayn to establish a barrier. The Syriac Alexander Legend has local elders describe the northern raiders, naming Gog and Magog among their kings, and Alexander orders an iron-and-brass gate to close the mountain pass.
records.similarity_note: Exact motifs checked in Budge's translated passage: named Gog and Magog as northern kings; danger to inhabitants; a mountain passage; an iron-and-brass barrier. Compare Qur'an 18:94–97, especially 18:94 and 18:96.
records.difference_note: The Syriac story explicitly identifies Alexander, locates the passage in a Roman-Persian imperial and Christian apocalyptic setting, and gives detailed dimensions and a key. The Qur'an calls the ruler Dhū al-Qarnayn, has the people offer payment and depicts a barrier built with iron and molten copper. Shared motifs do not prove direct textual borrowing or the ruler's historical identity.
records.source_edition: E. A. Wallis Budge (ed./trans.), The History of Alexander the Great: Being the Syriac Version of the Pseudo-Callisthenes (Cambridge University Press, 1889), vol. II, "A Christian Legend concerning Alexander," English pp. 151–154; cf. Corpus Coranicum, Q18:94 intertext 1475 and Q18:97 intertext 1417.
records.verification_note: 2026-11-02 batch 5: corrected an existing disputed row that conflated the Syriac Alexander Legend with the separate, later Apocalypse of Pseudo-Methodius. Checked E. A. Wallis Budge 1889 English translation pp. 151–154 as reproduced at the reference URL (local elders name Gog and Magog, and Alexander constructs the barrier). Cross-checked scholarly Corpus Coranicum Q18:94 intertext 1475 https://corpuscoranicum.org/en/verse-navigator/sura/18/verse/94/intertexts/1475 and Q18:97 intertext 1417 https://corpuscoranicum.de/de/verse-navigator/sura/18/verse/97/intertexts/1417. Budge's translation and modern online reproduction are not ancient manuscripts. Dating is debated and direct dependence is not established.

records.approx_date: Usually dated to the second century CE; surviving manuscript witnesses are later than the proposed composition.
records.source_locator: Protoevangelium of James §§10–11 (Mary returns home; annunciation at home)
records.parallel_summary: Qur’an 19:16 says Mary withdrew from her family to an eastern place before the encounter in 19:17–21. Protoevangelium of James §§10–11 describes Mary returning to her house, hearing a voice while fetching water, and meeting the angel in her house.
records.similarity_note: Both introduce Mary’s annunciation with a scene in which she is apart from others; the actual locations differ.
records.difference_note: Protoevangelium §§10–11 does not describe an eastern withdrawal; it locates the angelic appearance at Mary’s house after a trip to fetch water. Qur’an 19:16 explicitly mentions an eastern place, with the encounter in 19:17–21.
records.source_edition: New Advent English translation of Protoevangelium of James, §§10–11
records.verification_note: Checked Protoevangelium of James §§10–11 against Qur’an 19:16–21. This verse-specific entry is a contrast of the annunciation setting, NOT a claim that Protoevangelium supplies the eastern location or proves borrowing. Second-century composition estimate is not the date of extant manuscripts.

records.approx_date: Usually dated to the late first century CE (approximately 80–100 CE); surviving manuscripts are later; authorship and precise dating debated.
records.source_locator: Gospel of Luke 1:34 (read in context 1:26–38)
records.parallel_summary: Luke 1:34 records Mary asking the angel how conception can occur because she does not know a man. Qur’an 19:20 records Mary asking how she could have a son when no man has touched her and she has not been unchaste.
records.similarity_note: Both passages explicitly present Mary questioning how she can conceive without intercourse.
records.difference_note: Luke 1:35 answers with the Holy Spirit and calls the child the Son of God; Qur’an 19:21 emphasizes divine ease, a sign and mercy, without that designation. The accounts must not be treated as identical.
records.source_edition: King James Version, Luke 1:34–37, YouVersion Bible.com
records.verification_note: Checked the King James text of Luke 1:34–37 and Qur’an 19:20–21. Exact verse-level parallel is Mary’s question about conception without sexual relations; theological descriptions differ. Dating of the composition is separate from dates of extant witnesses; no direct literary dependence asserted.

records.approx_date: Probably 7th century CE; dating debated; earliest surviving manuscripts 9th century
records.source_locator: Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, chapter 20 (palm and water during flight to Egypt)
records.parallel_summary: Mary rests under a date palm; fruit becomes accessible and water emerges. Qur’an 19:23–25 features Mary at a palm during childbirth, a stream, and dates.
records.similarity_note: The palm tree, accessible fruit and nearby water occur in both narratives.
records.difference_note: Pseudo-Matthew places the event during the flight to Egypt with the young Jesus, not during childbirth; Jesus commands the palm and spring, whereas the Qur’an depicts divine aid to Mary.
records.source_edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. VIII, English translation of Pseudo-Matthew chapter 20 (Wikisource)
records.verification_note: Checked Pseudo-Matthew chapter 20 against Qur’an 19:23–25 and Corpus Coranicum TUK_459 (https://corpuscoranicum.de/en/verse-navigator/sura/19/verse/23/intertexts/459). The texts share motifs, but chronology and direct dependence are disputed; do not call this a demonstrably earlier source.

records.approx_date: Probably 7th century CE; dating debated; earliest surviving manuscripts 9th century
records.source_locator: Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, chapter 20 (palm and water during flight to Egypt)
records.parallel_summary: Pseudo-Matthew chapter 20 narrates a spring of water emerging at a palm tree; Qur’an 19:24 mentions a stream provided beneath Mary.
records.similarity_note: Both connect relief for Mary to water appearing at a palm-tree scene.
records.difference_note: In Pseudo-Matthew the child Jesus commands a spring during the flight to Egypt; the Qur’an places the stream at Jesus' birth and attributes the gift to Mary's Lord.
records.source_edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. VIII, English translation of Pseudo-Matthew chapter 20 (Wikisource)
records.verification_note: Read Pseudo-Matthew chapter 20 and Qur’an 19:24; the palm-water motif is a parallel, not a proven direct source. Compare Corpus Coranicum TUK_459; dating is disputed.

records.approx_date: Probably 7th century CE; dating debated; earliest surviving manuscripts 9th century
records.source_locator: Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, chapter 20 (palm and water during flight to Egypt)
records.parallel_summary: Pseudo-Matthew chapter 20 tells of Mary obtaining fruit from a palm tree when its branches bend; Qur’an 19:25 instructs Mary to shake the palm to obtain dates.
records.similarity_note: Both feature Mary obtaining fruit from a palm tree through extraordinary assistance.
records.difference_note: Pseudo-Matthew has the child Jesus command the palm to bend during flight to Egypt; Qur’an 19:25 instructs Mary herself to shake the trunk after childbirth.
records.source_edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. VIII, English translation of Pseudo-Matthew chapter 20 (Wikisource)
records.verification_note: Checked Pseudo-Matthew chapter 20 and Qur’an 19:25, with Corpus Coranicum TUK_459 for chronology; this is a motif parallel, not evidence of direct borrowing.

records.approx_date: The Book of Parables (1 Enoch 37–71) is commonly dated around the late first century BCE to first century CE, but its composition date remains debated. No Book of Parables fragments have been identified at Qumran. Its surviving Ethiopic witnesses and the 1912 English edition are later than its proposed composition.
records.source_type: Jewish apocalyptic literature / Enochic ascent narrative
records.source_locator: 1 Enoch 70:1–4 (R. H. Charles translation), especially 70:1–3; Book of Parables (1 Enoch 37–71)
records.parallel_summary: Qur’an 19:56–57 describes Idris as a truthful prophet whom God raised to a high station. In 1 Enoch 70:1–4 the figure Enoch is elevated from among earthly inhabitants, borne on chariots of the spirit, and placed in a heavenly realm. The identification of Idris with Enoch is found in later interpretation, not explicitly in the Qur’anic wording.
records.similarity_note: Specific motif verified: a righteous named figure elevated above earthly society. Compare Qur’an 19:57 with 1 Enoch 70:1–3. The identification Idris=Enoch is traditional and must not be treated as a Qur’anic statement.
records.difference_note: 1 Enoch supplies an elaborate ascent with chariots, winds and angels; Qur’an 19:57 says only that Idris was raised to a high station. 1 Enoch 70 includes Son of Man and Lord of Spirits language absent from this Qur’anic verse. Shared elevation imagery does not establish direct dependence.
records.source_edition: R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912), chapter 70:1–4; English text transcribed at Wikisource. For dating and Qumran absence: Devorah Dimant (2005), “The Book of Parables (1 Enoch 37–71) and the Qumran Scrolls,” Meghillot 3, pp. 49–67.
records.verification_note: 2026-11-02 batch 6: compared actual English text of 1 Enoch 70:1–4 (R. H. Charles edition) with Qur’an 19:56–57. Checked primary translation at https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Book_of_Enoch_(Charles)/Chapter_70 and scholarship on Parables dating and Qumran absence at https://cris.haifa.ac.il/en/publications/%D7%A1%D7%A4%D7%A8-%D7%94%D7%9E%D7%A9%D7%9C%D7%99%D7%9D-%D7%97%D7%A0%D7%95%D7%9A-%D7%94%D7%97%D7%91%D7%A9%D7%99-%D7%9C%D7%96-%D7%A2%D7%90-%D7%95%D7%9E%D7%92%D7%99%D7%9C%D7%95%D7%AA-%D7%A7%D7%95%D7%9E%D7%A8%D7%90%D7%9F/ . Verified as limited elevation-motif parallel only, NOT proof that Qur’anic Idris is textually identical to Enoch or that direct borrowing occurred. Later surviving manuscripts must not be conflated with proposed composition date.

records.approx_date: Composition date disputed; proposed dates span late antiquity to early medieval period
records.source_locator: Targum Sheni on Esther 1:2:8 (wild bird's report about Sheba)
records.parallel_summary: A wild bird reports to Solomon that a queen rules Sheba; Qur'an 27:22 has the hoopoe report news from Sheba.
records.similarity_note: Both contain a bird messenger bringing Solomon news about the Queen of Sheba.
records.difference_note: The Targum's broader tale includes elaborate royal and magical details; the Qur'an emphasizes monotheism. The Targum's date relative to the Qur'an is debated.
records.source_edition: Sefaria, Targum Sheni on Esther 1:2:8, with translation
records.verification_note: Matched Targum Sheni on Esther 1:2:8 to Qur'an 27:22. Dating of the Targum is disputed; this entry is a textual parallel, not proof of an earlier source or dependence.

records.approx_date: 3rd-5th century CE
records.source_locator: Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 12b:4–10 (Pharaoh's daughter and Moses)
records.parallel_summary: Sotah 12b discusses Pharaoh's daughter saving the infant Moses; Qur'an 28:9 identifies Pharaoh's wife as the one who asks that he not be killed.
records.similarity_note: Both involve a woman in Pharaoh's household protecting the infant Moses.
records.difference_note: The Talmud identifies Pharaoh's daughter, whereas the Qur'an identifies Pharaoh's wife. This is a substantive narrative difference.
records.source_edition: Sefaria, Babylonian Talmud Sotah 12b:4–10
records.verification_note: Verified the identity of Pharaoh's daughter in Sotah 12b:4–10; compared with the wife named by role in Qur'an 28:9. Classified as contrast, not identical account.

records.source_title: Book of Jubilees — The offering of Isaac
records.approx_date: Commonly dated to mid-second century BCE (precise dating debated). Earlier Hebrew manuscript fragments were found at Qumran; complete form is preserved in later Ethiopic witnesses. The linked R. H. Charles translation dates to 1913.
records.source_locator: Jubilees 18:1–2, 6–7
records.parallel_summary: God commands Abraham to offer his beloved son Isaac; Isaac asks about the sacrifice.
records.similarity_note: Both narrate Abraham's willingness to offer a son as sacrifice.
records.difference_note: Jubilees names Isaac and narrates a command; the Qur'an names no son and describes a dream and a reply showing assent.
records.source_edition: Book of Jubilees chs. 17–18, R. H. Charles English translation (1913), Christian Classics Ethereal Library; composition and translation dates distinguished.
records.verification_note: Checked 2026-11-08: Quran 37:102 against Jubilees 17–18, Charles translation (1913) at CCEL. This Second Temple work reworks Genesis 22 and names Isaac; the Quran passage does not name the son. Shared motifs do not prove direct dependence. Edition/manuscript/composition dates distinguished.

records.approx_date: Pre-Islamic Hebrew biblical narrative. Genesis developed through a debated ancient composition/redaction process (first millennium BCE); the modern JPS translation is from 2023, not the date of the original text.
records.source_locator: Genesis 22:1–2, 7–8
records.parallel_summary: God tests Abraham and directs him to offer his son Isaac; Isaac questions the sacrificial animal.
records.similarity_note: Both involve Abraham contemplating the sacrifice of his son under divine direction.
records.difference_note: Genesis names Isaac and describes a command; the Qur'an does not name the son in 37:102–107 and depicts a dream plus the son's assent.
records.source_edition: Sefaria, Genesis 22:1–19, Hebrew alongside Revised JPS English translation (2023).
records.verification_note: Checked 2026-11-08: Quran 37:102 read against Genesis 22 on Sefaria (Hebrew/Revised JPS). A specific text parallel or contrast, not evidence of direct borrowing. Isaac appears in Genesis but is unnamed in Quran 37:102–107; first millennium BCE formation is distinct from 2023 translation.

records.tradition: Second Temple Jewish / Qumran manuscript tradition
records.approx_date: Ancient Hebrew manuscript recovered from Qumran Cave 4 (deposited before 70 CE). Composition date and relationship to the Book of Jubilees remain debated; not the date of its 1994 or 2006 scholarly editions.
records.source_type: Fragmentary pre-Islamic Hebrew parabiblical manuscript; edited transcription with lacunae
records.source_locator: 4Q225 fragment 2, column i, lines 9–13 (Abraham, Isaac, Mastema's accusation and command)
records.parallel_summary: The preserved/reconstructed Hebrew retells the divine command that Abraham offer his son Isaac, with Mastema accusing Abraham concerning Isaac.
records.similarity_note: Both passages describe Abraham receiving a divine direction that imperils his son and initiates a test of obedience.
records.difference_note: 4Q225 explicitly names Isaac and depicts an instruction and Mastema's accusation; Qur'an 37:102 names no son, depicts Abraham's dream, and records the son's response. Bracketed reconstruction must not be treated as fully legible text.
records.source_edition: Joseph A. Fitzmyer, 'The Sacrifice of Isaac in Qumran Literature', Biblica 83 (2002), pp. 216–222 (transcribed/reconstructed Hebrew and analysis); compare James Kugel, 'Exegetical Notes on 4Q225 Pseudo-Jubilees', Dead Sea Discoveries 13 (2006), pp. 73–98, Brill preview https://brill.com/previewpdf/journals/dsd/13/1/article-p73_8.xml and VanderKam/Milik, DJD XIII (1994), 141–175.
records.verification_note: 2026-11-08: Checked Fitzmyer's published transcription and annotated translation of 4Q225 fr. 2 col. i 9–13 (Biblica 83 [2002], p. 216) and Kugel's printed transcription in Dead Sea Discoveries 13 (2006), p. 74. The ancient witness is fragmentary; additions inside editorial brackets are uncertain. The published primary-text transcription, rather than the original scroll, was inspected; no direct Quranic textual dependence inferred.

records.approx_date: Pre-Islamic Hebrew biblical narrative. Genesis developed through a debated ancient composition/redaction process (first millennium BCE); the modern JPS translation is from 2023, not the date of the original text.
records.source_locator: Genesis 22:9–10
records.parallel_summary: Abraham binds Isaac on the altar and takes a knife to sacrifice him.
records.similarity_note: Both recount preparations for a sacrifice before intervention.
records.difference_note: The Qur'an stresses both submitting and the son's forehead; Genesis depicts binding Isaac on an altar and does not record his verbal consent here.
